“In English, e is the letter that appears most often. The others follow in this order: a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z. The lead that e holds is so great that you will rarely find a sentence of any length in which some other letter appears more often.

“Right from the start, then, we have a basis for something better than a guess. The general purpose of this table is clear, though we will need only a little of its help with this particular code. Since 8 is the most common symbol here, we begin by supposing that it stands for the ordinary letter e. To test that idea, let us see whether 8 often appears twice together. A double e is very common in English, in words such as ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ and ‘agree.’ Although this coded message is short, we find a double 8 at least five times.

“Let us accept, then, that 8 means e. Next, ‘the’ is the most common word in English. We should therefore look for repeated groups of three symbols in the same order, with 8 as the last one. If we find such groups, they will very likely mean ‘the.’ Looking through the message, we discover no fewer than seven of them, all written ;48. We can now take ; to mean t, 4 to mean h, and 8 to mean e. That last idea has now received strong support. We have made a considerable advance.

“Once we have identified one word, we can work out something else of great importance: where several other words begin and end. Consider, for instance, the second-to-last appearance of ;48, near the end of the message. We know that the ; directly after it must start another word. Of the six symbols that follow this ‘the,’ we already understand five. Let us write them using the letters we know, leaving an empty space for the one we have not yet identified—

t eeth.

“We can immediately rule out the final ‘th’ as part of the word beginning with the first t. Try filling the empty space with each letter of the alphabet: no choice will produce a word that includes that final th. This leaves us with

t ee,

and if we go through the alphabet again, as before, we find that ‘tree’ is the only possible word.”

We declared ourselves free men with such volume and earnestness that the orator, with his mouth full of liberty, and his patriotic listeners began to take an interest. They closed around us with a most resolute air. The orator spoke:

“If ye are indeed free men, there is nothing for ye to dread—the liberties Heaven bestowed on Britain stand about ye as a shelter and a shield! (Applause.) Ye shall see presently. Produce your evidence.”

“Evidence of what?”

“That ye are free men.”

Ah—now I remembered! I recovered my senses and held my tongue. The king, however, burst out:

“Man, thou art mad. It would be more reasonable and just to require this rogue and thief to prove that we are not free.”

You see, he understood his laws as people so commonly understand laws: as words, without knowing their consequences. They acquire a meaning, and become wonderfully distinct, when they happen to be applied to you.

Everybody shook his head and appeared disappointed; a few lost interest and went away. The orator resumed, this time with a businesslike voice instead of an emotional one:

“If ye know not the laws of your own land, it is high time ye learnt them. Ye are unknown to us; that ye cannot deny. Perhaps ye are free men—we dispute it not; but perhaps ye are slaves. The law speaks plainly: the man who claims ye need not prove that ye are slaves; ye yourselves must prove that ye are not.”

I answered:

“My dear sir, only allow us time to send to Astolat; or let us send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good fellow. Such requests are extraordinary, and ye cannot expect them to be allowed. They would take much time, and impose an unjustified inconvenience on your master—”

“Master, fool!” thundered the king. “No man is my master; I myself am the m—”

“For God’s sake, be quiet!”

I spoke just quickly enough to halt him. We had difficulties enough; convincing these people that we were mad would improve nothing.

There is no point in spinning out the particulars. The earl offered us for sale and auctioned us off. That very same accursed law had prevailed in our own South in my own day, over thirteen centuries later. Under it, hundreds of free men, unable to establish their freedom, had been sold into slavery for life, a circumstance which had left no especially deep impression on me. Yet the moment I personally encountered the law and the auction block, what had formerly seemed merely wrong became downright hellish. Well, that is how we are constituted.

Yes, we went under the hammer, like pigs. A large town with a lively market would have fetched a respectable price for us; but business here was entirely dead, and the sum we brought still makes me blush whenever I remember it.

My heart beating with a fear for which I could find no cause, I sent the servant away, locked my door, and seated myself to read my father’s letter. Its words were these.

“My beloved Child,

“I have proved false to your trust; I have sought to corrupt your thoughts, and have taught your innocent heart the expressions and speech of an unnatural and forbidden passion. These offences demand expiation, and I must strive to make my punishment in some measure equal to my guilt. Doubtless you are ready for the announcement I must make: we must part, and remain parted for ever.

“I rob you of your father and your sole friend. I leave you without refuge in the world: your expectations are ruined, the serenity and safety of your untainted mind overthrown. Remembrance will show you dreadful pictures of guilt and the suffering of innocent affection deceived. Yet I, who bring this wretchedness upon you; I, who thrust you out, who have pitilessly impressed distrust and torment upon my own child’s heart and brow, and with a devil’s frivolity sought to take away her beauty and replace it with sin’s hideous deformity—I, in my heart’s overflowing distress, implore your forgiveness.

“I ask no pity; you must abhor me, and you do. But forgive me, Mathilda; do not send your thoughts after me into exile with anger that will never yield. I may never look on you again, never again listen to your voice; yet the gentle murmur of your pardon will come to me and soothe the fever of my distracted heart and brain. I believe that even in the grave I should feel it. I venture to urge my prayer by telling how unhappily I was drawn into this snare of burning misery, and how I struggled to escape. Indeed, were your soul less radiant and pure, I would not try to offer you any defence: I should dread that, in teaching you to view me with diminished horror, I might lessen your hatred of wickedness. But when I speak to you, I seem to plead before an angelic judge. Without your forgiveness I cannot go; I must seek to win it, or surrender to despair. Therefore I beseech you to hear me, and if, in the eyes of the good, guilt can be softened at all by piercing anguish and remorse that tears the mind like madness, perhaps you may believe, though I dare not, that I have some right to your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our earliest happy days beside Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of weary roaming, throughout which, despite the many perils and misfortunes I endured, my affections had remained a perfect blank.”
